On your own cluster (K3s or Kubernetes)

Source: vignettes/articles/install-cluster.Rmd
install-cluster.Rmd

This guide installs a lasting instance on a server you control: a virtual machine or a physical Linux host with single-node K3s, or an existing Kubernetes cluster. It was tested on Rocky Linux 8 and 9 and Ubuntu 24.04.

Read the Overview first for what each component does. For a host without internet access, combine this guide with Without internet access. For a cloud provider, see In the cloud.

1. Requirements

  • A Linux host you can sudo on, or an existing cluster and kubectl access to it.
  • For a host that will fit real studies: 8 CPUs or more, 16 to 32 GB of memory, and 100 GB of disk. The database (20 GB) and Dex (1 GB) volumes live on the node’s disk, next to the images. A smaller host (4 CPUs, 16 GB) is enough to bring the system up.
  • A hostname. It goes into every redirect URI, so choose it before you start (step 2).

On a new host, update the system and note its IP address:

sudo dnf -y update                                # Rocky
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get -y upgrade    # Ubuntu
ip -4 addr show | grep inet

2. Choose the hostname

The hostname must resolve to the node in three places: on the node, in the browsers that will use I-SPI, and inside the cluster.

  • With DNS: point an A record at the node. Without a domain, a wildcard DNS service such as sslip.io turns an IP into a name: 1-2-3-4.sslip.io resolves to 1.2.3.4.
  • Without DNS (a closed network): add the name to /etc/hosts on the node and to the hosts file of each client (C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows).

On K3s, pods resolve the name through coredns.yml (step 5), which the sed step fills in. Keep both values in shell variables:

export ISPI_HOST="ispi.example.org"   # the name users type in the browser
export ISPI_IP="1.2.3.4"              # the node's IP address

3. Install K3s (skip on an existing cluster) 

curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=v1.33.5+k3s1 sh -s - --disable=traefik
sudo ln -s /usr/local/bin/kubectl /bin/kubectl
sudo kubectl get node -o wide

--disable=traefik is required: this deployment brings its own Traefik. K3s keeps its built-in load balancer, which exposes Traefik on the node’s IP, and its local-path storage, which backs the volumes. The K3s requirements list what the host needs.

4. Namespace, cert-manager and a certificate authority 

sudo kubectl create ns immunoplex

sudo kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.19.1/cert-manager.yaml
sudo kubectl wait -n cert-manager --for=condition=ready pod -l app=webhook --timeout=5m

Every Ingress asks cert-manager for its certificate through the ClusterIssuer intermediate-ca1-issuer. The commands below create a private certificate authority with that issuer: a self-signed root, and an intermediate it signs. To use certificates browsers already trust instead, see In the cloud.

cat <<EOF | sudo kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: root-ca-issuer-selfsigned
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: root-ca
  namespace: cert-manager
spec:
  isCA: true
  commonName: root-ca
  secretName: root-ca-secret
  duration: 87600h # 10y
  renewBefore: 78840h # 9y
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
    rotationPolicy: Always
  issuerRef:
    name: root-ca-issuer-selfsigned
    kind: ClusterIssuer
    group: cert-manager.io
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: root-ca-issuer
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: root-ca-secret
EOF
sudo kubectl describe ClusterIssuer -n cert-manager     # root-ca-issuer should be Ready

cat <<EOF | sudo kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: intermediate-ca1
  namespace: cert-manager
spec:
  isCA: true
  commonName: intermediate-ca1
  secretName: intermediate-ca1-secret
  duration: 43800h # 5y
  renewBefore: 35040h # 4y
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
    rotationPolicy: Always
  issuerRef:
    name: root-ca-issuer
    kind: ClusterIssuer
    group: cert-manager.io
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: intermediate-ca1-issuer
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: intermediate-ca1-secret
EOF

# Copy the root certificate into the namespace, and export it for the browsers
sudo kubectl get secret root-ca-secret --namespace=cert-manager -o yaml \
  | sed 's/namespace: cert-manager/namespace: immunoplex/' \
  | sudo kubectl create -f -
sudo kubectl -n cert-manager get secret root-ca-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' \
  | base64 -d > immunoplex-root-ca.crt

Import immunoplex-root-ca.crt into the browser or operating-system trust store of every client. Without it, browsers warn that the site is not trusted.

5. Get and configure the manifests 

git clone https://github.com/immunoplex/i-spi-deployment.git
cd i-spi-deployment/k8s-manifests

The manifests contain placeholders (IMMUNOPLEX_*). One sed pass replaces each everywhere it appears, so values shared between files always match. Configuration and secrets lists what each placeholder is used for.

sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_HOSTNAME/$ISPI_HOST/g"                        *.yml
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_IP_ADDRESS/$ISPI_IP/g"                        coredns.yml
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_POSTGRES_PASSWORD/$(openssl rand -hex 16)/g"  *.yml
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID/$(openssl rand -hex 32)/g"    *.yml
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_OAUTH_SECRET/$(openssl rand -hex 32)/g"       *.yml
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_REDIS_AUTH/$(openssl rand -hex 32)/g"         *.yml
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_API_KEY/$(openssl rand -hex 32)/g"            *.yml
# only for the optional whoami test page:
sed -i "s/IMMUNOPLEX_OAUTH_COOKIE_SECRET/$(openssl rand -hex 16)/g" *.yml

Each sed line generates its value once and writes it into every file that uses it. The configured files now hold real secrets: keep them out of version control.

6. Deploy

Apply in order, and wait for each step before the next.

# Name resolution (K3s only) and the ingress
sudo kubectl apply -f coredns.yml
sudo kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy coredns
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex apply -f traefik.yml

# Sign-in
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex apply -f dex.yml

# Optional: test sign-in before going further (step 7)
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex apply -f whoami.yml
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=whoami --timeout=5m

# Database and schema (see Database schema)
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex apply -f postgresql.yml
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=postgresql --timeout=5m
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex exec -it deploy/postgresql -- psql -U postgres -c "CREATE DATABASE immunoplex;"
cat ../db/[0-9][0-9]_*.sql | sudo kubectl -n immunoplex exec -i deploy/postgresql -- \
  psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres immunoplex

# i-spi-compute, before I-SPI
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex apply -f i-spi-compute.yml
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=i-spi-compute-redis  --timeout=5m
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=i-spi-compute-api    --timeout=5m
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=i-spi-compute-worker --timeout=5m

# I-SPI (a large image; the first start can take several minutes)
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex apply -f i-spi.yml
sudo kubectl -n immunoplex wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=i-spi --timeout=10m

On a cluster that is not K3s, skip coredns.yml and make the hostname resolve through DNS instead.

7. Check that it works

  1. Sign-in (if you deployed whoami): open https://<host>/whoami, sign up, sign in, and check that the page shows your email address. Then remove the test page: sudo kubectl -n immunoplex delete -f whoami.yml.

  2. Database: sudo kubectl -n immunoplex exec -it deploy/postgresql -- psql -U postgres -c "select version();"

  3. Compute:

    sudo kubectl -n immunoplex exec -it deploy/i-spi-compute-api -- \
  python3 -c "import urllib.request; print(urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health').read().decode())"
# {"status":"ok","redis":"connected"}

  4. I-SPI: open https://<host>/i-spi/, sign in, create a project and a study, import plates and run a fit. When the results appear, the whole path works: I-SPI, the compute API, Redis, the worker, the database, and back.

If something does not work

  • Sign-in does not complete. Almost always a hostname mismatch. The hostname must be the same in the browser, the hosts files or DNS, coredns.yml and the manifests, and I-SPI’s APP_REDIRECT_URI (https://<host>/i-spi/) must be one of the client’s redirectURIs in dex.yml. Set SHINY_LOG_LEVEL to DEBUG in i-spi.yml and read kubectl -n immunoplex logs deploy/i-spi.
  • A fit is submitted but never finishes. Read the worker’s log: kubectl -n immunoplex logs deploy/i-spi-compute-worker. A stuck job is almost always on the compute side.
  • I-SPI cannot submit a job. From the I-SPI pod, curl http://i-spi-compute-api:8000/health should answer as in step 7. I-SPI and the API read the same key from the i-spi-compute Secret, so a 401 or 403 means the Secret changed after I-SPI started: restart I-SPI.
  • Fits are slow, or the worker is killed for lack of memory. Raise the worker’s CPU and memory limits in i-spi-compute.yml, keeping WORKER_CORES equal to the CPU limit, or add worker replicas.
  • The worker cannot reach the database. Its DB_SSLMODE must be require: PostgreSQL rejects connections without TLS.
  • A pod stays in ImagePullBackOff on a host without internet access: see Without internet access.

Remove it 

sudo kubectl delete ns immunoplex      # the application and its data
/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh        # or K3s and everything on it

Everything, including the database and the Dex accounts, is on the node. To keep results, pg_dump the immunoplex database first.
